Paragraphs.Text: A Finite-Resource Network Defense Decision Method Based on a Nonzero-Sum Differential Game

Abstract—To address cross-asset attack propagation and limited defense capacity in multi-asset networks, this paper establishes a complete-information, nonzero-sum, open-loop differential game. The network state is described by the compromised fraction of each asset to characterize how a defender dynamically deploys defensive resources. Continuous-time strategies are parameterized using piecewise-constant controls. By combining fourth-order Runge–Kutta integration, sequential least-squares programming, and alternating best responses, a dynamic defense action decision algorithm (ABR-DAD) is developed to calculate isolation and recovery intensities for each asset and time interval. A directed multi-asset propagation network is constructed to examine the spatiotemporal allocation of resources under different defense capacities. Dynamic defense, fixed-mean defense, and no defense are compared in terms of compromised states and cumulative losses under the same time-varying attack sequence. Simulations show that the computed plans satisfy per-time capacity constraints and yield differentiated resource allocation. Dynamic defense achieves lower cumulative weighted compromise loss and cumulative comprehensive defense loss than both reference schemes, demonstrating the effectiveness of the method for calculating dynamic defensive actions under finite resources.
Keywords— network defense decision-making, nonzero-sum differential game, alternating best response, attack propagation, resource allocation

A multi-asset network comprises interrelated logical assets, including entry services, business processing, identity authentication, and core data. Attacks can propagate from entry points to downstream assets along directed paths, causing compromise across multiple assets and business losses. A defender can suppress outgoing propagation through source-side isolation or reduce local compromise through recovery. These actions differ in security effects, business impacts, and resource consumption. Under limited capacity, the defender must account for the attacker’s strategy when determining the type, intensity, and timing of defensive actions.

Regarding network propagation control and resource allocation, Preciado et al.[1] studied the allocation of protection resources to inhibit spreading processes in directed networks. Al-Eiadeh and Abdallah[2] allocated defense resources to interdependent systems using attack graphs and PageRank. Paarporn and Xu[3] examined resource tradeoffs between preventive and reactive defenses, while Chen et al.[4] investigated the effects of protection and recovery investments and node priorities on network robustness. These studies provide a basis for characterizing propagation structure, asset importance, and defense costs.

In network attack–defense games, Shao and Li[5] used a multistage attack–defense graph to examine resource allocation during sequential attacks. Hu et al.[6] optimized moving-target defense through a Markov differential game, and Lou et al.[7] studied dynamic collaborative defense in crowdsensing networks under incomplete information. Huang and Zhu[8] used a susceptible–infected–susceptible (SIS) propagation model and a differential-game framework to study virus suppression and adaptive adjustment of connection weights in complex networks. Mi et al.[9] introduced stochastic disturbances into network attack–defense state evolution and developed a stochastic differential-game model for defense strategy selection. Tian et al.[10] studied a nonzero-sum attack–defense game for malware propagation in cloud environments. Zhang et al. investigated real-time defense in scale-free networks[11] and potential differential-game decisions in complex networks[12]. Sun et al.[13] incorporated action and timing choices into a time differential game. These works provide methodological foundations for analyzing strategic interactions alongside network-state evolution.

For post-attack repair, Yang et al.[14] employed a differential game to study host repair under advanced persistent threats (APTs). Wang et al.[15] examined APT lateral movement, repair delays, and resource constraints in time-varying networks. Qin et al.[16] studied defense outsourcing under limited budgets through an impulsive differential game. Existing work thus covers propagation control, strategic interaction, and dynamic repair. This study further addresses the joint spatiotemporal allocation of source-side isolation and local recovery in a directed propagation network under attacker strategy responses and finite capacity constraints.

This paper undertakes three tasks: constructing a nonzero-sum, open-loop differential-game model involving directed propagation, source-side isolation, and local recovery; designing ABR-DAD using piecewise-constant controls and alternating best responses to compute defensive actions by asset and interval; and analyzing allocations across defense capacities while comparing dynamic, fixed-mean, and no-defense plans under a common attack sequence in terms of compromised states and cumulative losses.

Isolation acts on outgoing propagation from a source asset, whereas recovery reduces local compromise. Their effectiveness depends on propagation links, compromised states, and the remaining planning horizon.

A complete-information, two-player, noncooperative, nonzero-sum, open-loop differential game is defined on the continuous-time state system. At the planning origin, both players know the network topology, initial state, model parameters, objective functions, and constraints, and separately choose open-loop control plans over the horizon.

Equations (13)–(14) describe each player’s best response to a fixed opponent plan and form the basis of alternating optimization. Fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) integration[19] evaluates candidate plans; sequential least-squares programming (SLSQP) solves the single-player optimization with control bounds and linear capacity constraints[20,21]. The plans are then updated alternately. The final strategies undergo deviation searches from multiple initializations, constraint checks, and integration-refinement tests. The state equation evaluates compromise evolution under a control plan, while the finite-dimensional controls correspond directly to the defense locations, intervals, and intensities that the defender must determine.

Based on the best-response principle for dynamic noncooperative games[17] and related iterative work[22], we design Alternating Best Response for Dynamic Defense Action Decision (ABR-DAD). Its purpose is to produce a defense action plan: holding the attack plan fixed, optimize isolation and recovery; then, holding the defense plan fixed, compute the attack response; and alternate until the numerical stopping conditions are met. The API gateway serves as an attack entry point and connects to order processing and identity authentication, so isolation and recovery are applied together in early intervals. Figure 4 shows the API gateway, identity authentication, core database, and network value-weighted compromised fractions under the same attack sequence; Table 3 summarizes the metrics. At the beginning of interval 6 (𝑡≈8.33), gateway entry attack intensity declines from 0.384142 to 0.139831 and Web entry intensity from 0.365943 to 0.137174. Under all three schemes, newly induced compromise pressure on the gateway falls below the corresponding recovery effect, changing its compromised fraction from increasing to decreasing. Identity authentication and the core database remain affected by upstream propagation and continue to accumulate compromise, illustrating propagation lag.

Dynamic defense allocates more isolation and recovery to the gateway during early and middle intervals, reducing accumulated compromise earlier. In the final interval, its gateway recovery intensity is 0.080739, below approximately 0.262580 for fixed-mean defense. Consequently, the gateway compromised fraction decreases faster under the fixed scheme and becomes lower than under the dynamic scheme after 𝑡≈8.49. A late crossover also occurs for identity authentication, whereas the core database maintains a lower compromised fraction under dynamic defense. The network value-weighted compromised fraction is lower under dynamic defense during most of the horizon, but slightly lower under fixed defense at the terminal time. Cumulative loss and terminal state must therefore be distinguished.

Table 3 reports cumulative comprehensive defense losses of 10.945701, 9.556834, and 9.326647 for no defense, fixed-mean defense, and dynamic defense, respectively. The dynamic scheme reduces this loss by approximately 14.79% and 2.41% relative to the two alternatives. Under the same attack sequence and equal per-asset cumulative control inputs, adjusting the timing of isolation and recovery reduces cumulative weighted compromise loss by 0.403329 relative to fixed-mean defense. Although the dynamic scheme incurs greater business and action costs and a slightly higher terminal network weighted compromised fraction than fixed-mean defense, its reduction of early accumulated compromise produces a lower overall comprehensive loss. Hence, the timing of defense actions substantially influences network-state evolution and cumulative protection effectiveness.

At the terminal time, the fixed scheme has a slightly lower network weighted compromised fraction than the dynamic scheme, and both improve on no defense. Figure 4 also shows that dynamic defense better protects the core database at the terminal time, whereas fixed defense yields lower terminal compromised fractions at the API gateway and identity authentication. Thus, terminal compromise and cumulative loss reflect distinct evaluation dimensions. Overall, the computed dynamic plan reduces cumulative compromise and comprehensive defense losses by appropriately timing its actions, without implying minimum compromise for every asset at every instant.

This paper establishes a nonzero-sum, open-loop differential-game model that incorporates rational attack choices and cross-asset propagation, and proposes ABR-DAD for dynamic defense action decision-making. Simulations show that the algorithm produces differentiated allocations across time intervals and assets under all three defense capacities. Under the same attack sequence, dynamic defense reduces cumulative comprehensive defense loss relative to both no defense and fixed-mean defense, and mitigates compromise accumulation at entry and key internal assets during most intervals. Late crossovers in certain asset states further indicate the need to evaluate defense plans using a comprehensive objective encompassing time-accumulated compromise and action costs. Future work will calibrate propagation rates and defense costs using measured security-operation data and extend network scale and execution feedback to assess defense-plan updates under real operational conditions.
